issues.legal_issue: The government's relinquishment of property previously taken under an act of state constituted a fresh inam grant, making the property an estate under the applicable land-tenure law.
material_facts: After the ruler died without a male heir, the East India Company took possession of all his properties, including his private property.
In 1862, the Government of India sanctioned relinquishment of the landed property in favour of the ruler's heirs.
The disputed lands were part of the property derived from that relinquishment.
issues.conclusion: The 1862 relinquishment was a fresh grant, not a restoration of antecedent rights, and the property qualified as an estate under section 3(2)(d) of the Madras Estates Land Act.
issues.legal_principle: Where an act of state extinguishes existing rights in property, its later relinquishment by the government in favour of former claimants is a fresh grant rather than a revival of those rights. The Court applied section 3(2)(d) of the Madras Estates Land Act and relied on Jijoyiamba Bayi Saiba v. Kamakshi Bayi Saiba, Sundaram Ayyar v. Ramachandra Ayyar, Maharaja of Kolhapur v. Sundaram Iyer, Sundaram v. Deva Sankara, and T. R. Bhavani Shankar Joshi v. Somasundra Moopanar.

predicates.inam_estate_classification_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether land belongs to an estate formed by an inam grant.
predicates.government_relinquished_property_after_a: After the government had taken property under an act of state, it relinquished that property in favour of former claimants.

issues.definition: When an estate-classification dispute concerns property relinquished by the government after an act of state, the property derives from a fresh inam grant.

issues.legal_issue: An area granted as an inam qualifies as an estate under the applicable land-tenure law when it constitutes a whole village.
material_facts: Revenue accounts and other records identified Orathur Padugai as a separate village over an extended period.
Leases, rent receipts, and sale deeds also described Orathur Padugai as a village.
The lower courts found that the disputed lands were within that village, and the Supreme Court held that finding was supported by the evidence.
issues.conclusion: Orathur Padugai was a whole village and therefore an estate within the meaning of section 3(2)(d) of the Act.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 3(2)(d), an inam village may constitute an estate; whether the granted area is a whole village is determined from the evidence in the particular case. Section 3(19) defines a village by reference to designation in revenue accounts and separate maintenance of revenue accounts, among other criteria. The Court relied on the revenue records and related documents identifying the area as a village.

issues.legal_issue: Cultivable land in an inam village is ryoti land rather than private land when the landholder fails to establish personal cultivation or retention for personal use.
material_facts: The landholder owned both warams in the disputed lands, but the Court held that this fact alone did not establish that the lands were private.
There was no proof that the landholder had directly cultivated the lands or retained them for personal use and cultivation under personal supervision.
Tenants continued to cultivate the lands without a break or change, notwithstanding periodic auctions of lease rights.
The lands were not recorded as private land, and the landholder did not rebut the statutory presumption that land in an inam village was not private land.
issues.conclusion: The disputed lands were ryoti lands, not private lands; the appeals were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 3(10)(b) and 3(16) distinguish private land from cultivable ryoti land. The ordinary test for private land is retention by the landholder for personal use and cultivation by the landholder or under personal supervision; ownership of both warams and short-term letting alone do not suffice. Section 185 presumes that land in an inam village is not private land until the contrary is proved. Section 6 gives a ryot in possession of ryoti land a permanent right of occupancy. The Court relied on Yerlagadda Malikarjuna Prasad Nayudu v. Somayya.
